title: What is the difference between HPA (replica count by metrics), VPA (per-pod CPU/memory), Cluster Autoscaler (node count), and KEDA (event/queue-driven scaling), and can HPA and VPA be used together safely?
shortTitle: HPA vs VPA vs Cluster Autoscaler vs KEDA, and Combining HPA with VPA

s1_definition.profdef: These are four different autoscalers operating at different layers. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) changes the NUMBER of Pod replicas based on metrics like CPU, memory, or custom metrics. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) changes the CPU and memory requests and limits of each Pod. The Cluster Autoscaler changes the NUMBER of NODES when Pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) scales replicas based on external event sources like a Kafka lag or a queue depth, and can scale to zero. HPA and VPA must not both manage the same CPU or memory metric on the same workload, but they can coexist if VPA handles memory while HPA scales on a different signal.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, HPA is opening MORE identical counters when the queue of customers grows. VPA is giving each existing teller a BIGGER desk and more tools because their work got heavier. Cluster Autoscaler is building MORE floors in the branch when there is no room for new counters. KEDA is watching the overnight batch of pending settlements in a queue and opening counters exactly in proportion to how many files are waiting, even down to zero counters when the queue is empty. You cannot have two managers both deciding counter count based on the same CPU meter, or they fight.
s1_definition.oneliner: HPA scales replicas out, VPA scales each Pod up, Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, KEDA scales on events to zero, and HPA plus VPA on the same CPU metric conflict.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are four different autoscalers operating at different layers. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) changes the NUMBER of Pod replicas based on metrics like CPU, memory, or custom metrics. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) changes the CPU and memory requests and limits of each Pod. The Cluster Autoscaler changes the NUMBER of NODES when Pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) scales replicas based on external event sources like a Kafka lag or a queue depth, and can scale to zero. HPA and VPA must not both manage the same CPU or memory metric on the same workload, but they can coexist if VPA handles memory while HPA scales on a different signal.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, HPA is opening MORE identical counters when the queue of customers grows. VPA is giving each existing teller a BIGGER desk and more tools because their work got heavier. Cluster Autoscaler is building MORE floors in the branch when there is no room for new counters. KEDA is watching the overnight batch of pending settlements in a queue and opening counters exactly in proportion to how many files are waiting, even down to zero counters when the queue is empty. You cannot have two managers both deciding counter count based on the same CPU meter, or they fight.

**One line to remember:** HPA scales replicas out, VPA scales each Pod up, Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, KEDA scales on events to zero, and HPA plus VPA on the same CPU metric conflict.

sections.s2_technical:
The HPA watches a metric and compares it to a target. With a CPU target of seventy percent, if average CPU utilization climbs, the HPA increases the replica count, and when it falls it scales back down within the configured minimum and maximum. HPA can also use memory, custom application metrics through the custom metrics API, or external metrics. This is the workhorse for stateless banking services like the Transfer API, where more load simply needs more identical Pods.

The VPA recommends and optionally applies right-sized CPU and memory requests for each Pod by observing actual usage over time. In `Auto` or `Recreate` mode it evicts and recreates Pods with the new requests, which causes a restart, so for latency-sensitive services many teams run VPA in `Off` (recommendation-only) mode and apply the numbers at deploy time. VPA is ideal for workloads whose per-Pod footprint is hard to guess, like a nightly reconciliation job.

The Cluster Autoscaler operates on the infrastructure layer. When the scheduler cannot place a Pod because no node has enough free CPU or memory, the Pod goes `Pending`, and the Cluster Autoscaler adds a node to the node group so the Pod can schedule. When nodes sit underutilized, it drains and removes them to save cost. It is reactive to unschedulable Pods, which is why HPA and Cluster Autoscaler work as a pair: HPA creates more Pods, and if they do not fit, Cluster Autoscaler creates more nodes.

KEDA extends HPA with event-driven scalers. Instead of CPU, KEDA reads a source such as Kafka consumer lag, an SQS queue length, a Prometheus query, or a cron schedule, and drives the replica count from that. Crucially KEDA can scale a Deployment to zero when there is no work and back up when events arrive, which pure HPA cannot do. For a banking settlement consumer that only has work when files land on a queue, KEDA scales from zero to many consumers based on the backlog, then back to zero, saving cost overnight.

On combining HPA and VPA: the hard rule is that they must not both act on the same resource metric for the same workload, because HPA would add replicas to reduce per-Pod CPU while VPA simultaneously shrinks per-Pod CPU requests, and they oscillate against each other. The safe patterns are: run VPA in recommendation-only mode and let HPA own scaling, or let VPA manage memory while HPA scales on CPU or a custom metric, so each autoscaler owns a distinct signal. VPA and Cluster Autoscaler combine naturally because larger Pod requests simply trigger more nodes.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India we run two very different workloads, and each needs a different autoscaler. Three real problems drove the design.

Problem 1 — the Transfer API gets unpredictable spikes at salary time when thousands of customers move money at once. We cannot pre-provision for the peak or we waste money all month. This is exactly what HPA solves — it watches CPU and adds Transfer Pods during the spike and removes them afterward.

Problem 2 — the overnight Settlement Consumer only has work when settlement files land on a queue; most of the night the queue is empty. Running Pods idle all night wastes money. This is exactly what KEDA solves — it scales the consumer from zero up to the backlog and back to zero.

Problem 3 — a new Fraud Scoring service kept getting OOM-killed because we guessed its memory wrong. This is exactly what VPA (recommendation mode) solves — it observes real usage and tells us the right request, while HPA still scales replicas on CPU, so the two never fight.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of four autoscalers: an `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` driven by CPU, a `VerticalPodAutoscaler` that recommends memory, a `ClusterAutoscaler` that adds nodes when Pods are Pending, and a `KedaScaler` driven by queue depth that can reach zero. We feed them a workload for the Transfer API and the Settlement Consumer using the `Account` model for Rajesh and Priya and log each scaling decision.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a salary-day spike on the Transfer API, a memory observation for Fraud Scoring, and an overnight queue for the Settlement Consumer.

Step 1 — The Transfer API starts at 2 replicas. CPU jumps to 140 percent against a 70 percent target, so HPA computes a desired replica count of 4 (2 times 140 over 70) and scales out. Rajesh's fifty-thousand-rupee transfer to Priya is served comfortably across the 4 replicas.

Step 2 — Those 4 Pods need capacity. The Cluster Autoscaler sees that 4 Pods at 4 Pods-per-node need 1 node and keeps 1 node. If the spike had pushed replicas to 10, the Cluster Autoscaler would add nodes so the extra Pods schedule.

Step 3 — The spike ends and CPU falls to 30 percent. HPA scales back toward the minimum of 2 replicas, and the Cluster Autoscaler trims idle nodes.

Step 4 — For Fraud Scoring, the VPA observes memory peaks of 430, 610, and 520 MiB. It takes the peak of 610, adds 25 percent headroom, rounds to a 64-MiB boundary, and recommends a 768-MiB request. Because VPA is only recommending memory while HPA scales on CPU, the two never conflict.

Step 5 — For the Settlement Consumer, KEDA sees an empty queue overnight and holds 0 replicas, saving cost. When a batch of 480 messages lands, KEDA scales to the ceiling of 480 over 50, which is 10 replicas. Once drained back to 0, KEDA returns the Deployment to 0 replicas.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes autoscaling happens at four distinct layers, and naming them precisely is what an interviewer wants to hear. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of Pod replicas based on a metric such as CPU, memory, or a custom application metric, so it scales a stateless service out and in with load. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes the CPU and memory requests of each individual Pod based on observed usage, so it right-sizes a workload whose footprint is hard to guess. The Cluster Autoscaler changes the number of nodes, adding capacity when Pods cannot be scheduled and reclaiming nodes when they sit idle. KEDA is event-driven autoscaling that reads an external source like Kafka lag or a queue depth, drives replicas from that, and uniquely can scale all the way down to zero.

These layers naturally combine in pairs. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and the Cluster Autoscaler are a classic team: the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler creates more Pods for load, and if those Pods do not fit on existing nodes, the Cluster Autoscaler provisions more nodes. KEDA sits on top of the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler machinery but adds event sources and scale-to-zero, which is perfect for bursty background work.

The question of combining the Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers has a sharp answer: never let both manage the same resource metric on the same workload. If the Horizontal autoscaler adds replicas to bring per-Pod CPU down while the Vertical autoscaler simultaneously shrinks per-Pod CPU requests, they oscillate against each other and the workload never stabilizes. They coexist safely only when each owns a different signal, for example the Vertical autoscaler managing memory in recommendation mode while the Horizontal autoscaler scales on CPU or a custom metric.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used all four deliberately. The stateless Transfer API ran on the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler driven by CPU, paired with the Cluster Autoscaler so salary-day spikes got both more Pods and more nodes. The Fraud Scoring service used the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode to fix the memory requests we had been guessing wrong, while the Horizontal autoscaler still scaled it on CPU, so the two never fought. And the overnight Settlement Consumer used KEDA on Kafka lag so it sat at zero replicas when the queue was empty and scaled up only when a batch of files arrived, which cut our idle overnight compute cost dramatically.
